assen-totin-oric-tape-readme.text:
This is a small programme which converts a data file (usually a tape or disk
image) into a sound representation (WAV file) and back.


DATA-TO-WAV CONVERSION
======================

Use od2w. Give it the source and target file names. It will produce a 44.1 kHz 
mono WAV file from your data file.

The produced WAV file can be played via a standard PC sound card and fed to 
the tape (cassette deck) input of Oric Atmos 8 bit PC (or any of its clones 
like Pravetz 8D).

The WAV file is encoded as if it was written by the 8-bit PC at 300 bps 
(usually callsed 'slow' mode). Hence, the PC should be set to loading in slow 
mode. For Oric, load with the following comand: 

CLOAD "",S

The actual data will be preceded by a few seconds of Oric sync sequence, 0x16. 
Do note that Oric expects some header information rearding the content type
(BASIC code, machine code etc.), autoplay (on or off) and memory address to
load the programme to; you have to provide this header in your data file. 


WAV-TO-DATA CONVERSION
======================

Use ow2d. Give it a source and target file names. It will produce a binary 
representation of your WAV file.

The WAV file can be recorded from the audio output of Oric Atmos. The WAV file 
should be 44.1 kHz, mono. It should begin with the Oric Atmos sync sequence
(several seconds of 0x16) followed by the Oric header. Only if these two are
present the decoding will be successful. 

The recording should be done in 'slow' mode (300 bps). For Oric Atmos, the 
command to save the file is:

CSAVE "SOME_PROG_NAME",S

Regarding saving BASIC programs, do note that Oric stores the program operators
not by their name (e.g., PRINT), but by thei relevant hex code. The ow2d will 
not convert such hex codes back into BASIC operators; you should do this 
manually if you need it.

hippietrail-disgpl-readme-md.text:
Graphic Programming Language disassembler
=========================================

This is an ISO C99 implementation of a disassembler for the
Texas Instruments "Graphic Programming Language", used in the
TI-99/4A.

It disassembles both standard GPL opcodes and FMT opcodes.
The mnemonics of FMT opcodes seem poorly standardized, but I'm using
those from [Thierry Nouspikel's GPL page](
https://www.unige.ch/medecine/nouspikel/ti99/gpl.htm).

Note that the operand order `OPCODE src,dest` is used by this
disassembler.  This matches the order used by Thierry's assembler, but
differs from the disassemblies printed in the TI99/4A INTERN book by
Heiner Martin.


Building
--------

A trivial `Makefile` is included for building the disassembler, but
really just compiling the single source file with any C compiler should
do.  :-)



Usage
-----

The `disgpl` program takes two to four arguments:

```
disgpl file base_addr [start_addr] [func_info_file]
```

The first argument is the file containing the binary dump of the GROM(s)
to disassemble.  The second argument is the base address corresponding
to the first byte of the file, in hexadecimal.  The third argument
specifies the address at which to start the disassembly, in hexadecimal.
This argument is optional and if omitted the base address will be used
as the address at which to start disassembly.  Typically you will want
to specify an address past the GROM headers.

The fourth and last argument is a file containing information about the
amount of `FETC` data various subroutines requires.  This allows the
disassembler to display this data as `DATA` directives following the
`CALL` opcode, instead of incorrectly disassembling this data as GPL
instructions.  The file should contain lines each containing first
the address of a GPL subroutine, as hexadecimal, and then a colon,
and finally the number of bytes of data that follows a call to the
subroutine at that address.  An example of such a file follows:

```
0010 : 1
001e : 4
14a9 : 1
2010 : 4
284c : 2
284e : 2
2d99 : 2
30b9 : 1
4cb9 : 1
```

The fourth argument can be omitted, in which case no special handling
of `FETC` data is performed.

Related Projects
================

- [xdt99/xdg99](https://github.com/endlos99/xdt99?tab=readme-ov-file#xda99)

matejjan-png-to-scr-readme-md.text:
## PNG to SCR online converter

PNG to SCR is a tool for artists that create ZX Spectrum artworks in the usual (pixel art) graphics software such as Photoshop, GIMP, Aseprite, Pixaki etc. 

It allows you to take the exported PNG file and convert it into a SCR (video memory dump) or TAP that you can load into a real (or emulated) machine with `LOAD "" $SCREEN`.

Online build: [www.retronator.com/png-to-scr](http://www.retronator.com/png-to-scr)

Main user interface:

![](http://i.imgur.com/miTt1MJ.png)

Every spectrum image has multiple alternatives in which ink/color choices to make, so the tool has options on the strategy to use.

Match mode (pictured above) tries to create something close to what an artist would manually choose (preserving same-colored shapes as much as possible).

Bigger area + Paper for single blocks (or Smaller area + Ink) gives you something that looks like lineart (tries to use minimum pixels covered with ink):

![](http://i.imgur.com/PMGYfYA.png)

When you manually try to conform to attribute clash, it's hard to catch everything, so the tool gives you error detection:

![](http://i.imgur.com/WzmaoJo.gif)

As you can see above it supports images of non-screen dimensions. However, the conversion will happen only on a screen-sized region:

![](http://i.imgur.com/YOLv9uk.png)

When I get some more time (and need) I will add the user interface to select a custom cropped area.

It's also missing support for non-screen images that don't have the attribute grid aligned to 0,0.

The online version doesn't have the "Preview TAP" feature yet even though you can see it in these screenshots (from development build).

The images in the screenshots are [my works](http://retronator.deviantart.com/gallery/36226378/Pixel-Art).

Converts ZX Spectrum SCR file to TRS-80 charset map, which can be loaded to screen memory as characters

cd build
cmake ../CMakeLists.txt
make

scr2trs -i <in_filename> -o <out_filename> [-h]

jhonnyb01-m68k-simulator-readme-md.text:
# 68K Sim — Motorola 68000 Assembler & Simulator for iOS

> An iOS app that turns your iPhone into a **Motorola 68000** computer.
> You write real 68000 assembly, an assembler built from scratch turns it into
> machine code, and you **step through it one instruction at a time** on an
> accurate CPU core — watching the registers, memory and console change.

Built solo. Shipped to TestFlight / the App Store.

---

## The idea

Computer Architecture courses still teach the 68000, and the standard tool
(EASy68K) is Windows-only. There was nothing decent to practise on from a phone.
So: a full 68000 workstation in your pocket — editor, two-pass assembler,
step debugger, register and memory inspectors, and EASy68K-style `TRAP #15`
console I/O so the exercises from class run unchanged.

---

## What it demonstrates

| Area | Skill shown |
|------|-------------|
| **Emulator integration** | Vendored the **Musashi** 68000 C core (the one used in MAME) and generated its opcode tables; wrote the memory bus, reset-vector setup and the run / single-step / breakpoint loop in C. |
| **Systems programming (C)** | Big-endian 16 MiB memory bus; EASy68K `TRAP #15` console I/O (16 tasks); and a **"monitor" trick** — every CPU exception vector is pointed at an `ILLEGAL` opcode in a reserved page, so an unhandled 68000 exception (odd address, /0, privilege…) lands there and can be caught in the illegal-instruction callback and reported with its vector number. |
| **Compiler back end** | A **two-pass assembler in Swift**: line parser, recursive-descent expression evaluator (`$`/`%`/`@` bases, `*` = location counter), symbol table, and an instruction encoder that emits correct 68000 machine code for **all standard addressing modes** and the taught instruction set, with clear line-numbered diagnostics. |
| **Swift ↔ C interop** | `@convention(c)` callback trampolines carrying an `Unmanaged` context pointer; bridging the C core's I/O callbacks to a Swift `EmulatorIO` protocol; **blocking the emulator thread on a semaphore** while the UI collects a line of console input, then resuming. |
| **SwiftUI** | Multi-panel debugger UI — source editor, live D0–D7 / A0–A7 / PC / SR with change highlighting, hex memory viewer, disassembly listing with tap-to-toggle breakpoints, console, and a built-in theory reference. |
| **Tooling** | XcodeGen-generated project; the core is a Swift Package that runs its full test suite on macOS with **no simulator** (`swift test`); scripted archive → export → TestFlight upload via the App Store Connect API. |

---

## What's in this repo

A **portfolio excerpt** — the files that carry the interesting engineering, not
the whole app:

- [`m68kbridge.c`](m68kbridge.c) / [`m68kbridge.h`](m68kbridge.h) — the C glue to the Musashi core: RAM, `TRAP #15`, the exception-monitor trick, and run/step/breakpoint control.
- [`Encoder.swift`](Encoder.swift) — the heart of the assembler: effective-address encoding for every 68000 mode, and per-mnemonic machine-code generation (bit-field packing, PC-relative displacement math, pass-1/pass-2 duality).
- [`Assembler.swift`](Assembler.swift) — the two-pass driver: line parsing, label/symbol resolution, directives (`ORG`, `EQU`, `DC`, `DS`, …), and coalescing the output into loadable segments.
- [`Emulator.swift`](Emulator.swift) — the Swift wrapper around the C core and the I/O bridge.

The SwiftUI app shell, the full (~2000-line) instruction set, the tutorial /
theory content and the StoreKit layer are intentionally omitted.

---

## Requirements

- Xcode 16+, iOS 16+
- The core (assembler + emulator) builds and tests on macOS with `swift test` — no device or simulator needed.

---

*Built solo with Swift, C and SwiftUI.
CPU core: [Musashi](https://github.com/kstenerud/Musashi) © Karl Stenerud, MIT license.*

dj-on-github-py6502-readme-txt.text:
A python based 6502 assembler, disassembler and simulator
David Johnston

The Philosophy
--------------

I enjoy old-school electronics and programming. I've learned over time that there is a benefit to combining old-school methods with modern tools.

For example:
1) My day job is a chip designer, focusing on cryptgraphic circuits. For a particular project I either needed a big state machine or a small CPU. An old school 8 bit processor took me 4 hours to implement in synthesizable RTL and on a modern silicon process it runs blindingly fast in a tiny bit of silicon area. It came with lots of tools already since the instruction set was standard.

2) I wrote a Point-of-Sale system for a family store, since the off-the-shelf solutions were expensive and none of them matched the needs of the store. Instead of going for some windows interface or touch driven app on a tablet, I wrote the user interface using the old-school curses library for a text based interface that was designed to minimize keystrokes at the checkout. The staff loved it since the key strokes took a couple of minutes to learn and I wrote it in Python, bringing the simplicity and power of modern programming tools.

In both cases, the benefits of the efficiencies of old school methods with the power of modern methods yielded something better than either.

This project is a proof-of-concept for this idea. I use it for hacking my Apple //e.  It's a 6502 assembler, disassembler and simulator written in Python. Many old 6502 assemblers exist, but they suffer from inconsistent formats, directives and macro processors. In particular the macro processors tended to be horrible.

The thing that makes it a little different is that instead of offering a 'better assembler language' or 'better macro language' I've stripped down the programs to the very basic functions but written them such that they are intended to be called from a python program that feeds it assembler and gets object code back. This then makes python the macro language. So you get the ability to write assembly code normally, or you can write python to automate the code generation or generate parameterized code, or unroll loops or any number of other things, but using a nice language that makes it easy rather than a set of confusing macro directive written in 1978.

If you want to instrument and test of a bit of code, it's easy to assemble it and then write a program in python to iterate over your chosen input states and check the outputs and simulate the code repeatedly, calling the simulation of each instruction directly from python, coding in whatever analysis meets your needs.

The simulator and disassembler works directly with the object code and symbol table from the assembler.

An Simple Example: Sending Assembly to the Assembler From Python
----------------------------------------------------------------
This python (see src/small_example.py) assembles a few instructions

from asm6502 import asm6502

        thecode = """
                ORG  $100
        start:
                LDA #$10
                LDX #$00
        loop:
                STA $1000,x
                INX
                SBC #$01
                BPL loop
                RTS
        """
        
        lines = thecode.splitlines()
        
        a = asm6502()
        (lst,sym)= a.assemble(lines)
        # inspect output..
        for line in lst:
            print(line)
        print()
        for symbol in sym:
            print(symbol)
        print()
        a.print_object_code()

The output looks like this:
        LISTING
        1    0000 :                                
        2    0100 :                  org $100      
        3    0100 : start:                         
        4    0100 :         A9 10    lda #$10      
        5    0102 :         A2 00    ldx #$00      
        6    0104 : loop:                          
        7    0104 :         9D 00 10 sta $1000,x   
        8    0107 :         E8       inx           
        9    0108 :         E9 01    sbc #$01      
        10   010A :         10 F8    bpl loop      
        11   010C :         60       rts           
        12   010D :   
        
        SYMBOL TABLE
        start      = $0100
        loop       = $0104
        
        OBJECT CODE
        *
        0100: A9 10 A2 00 9D 00 10 E8 E9 01 10 F8 60         
        *

The Listing
-----------

If after running that, you typed this:
    >>> a.listing

you would see the assembly output as an array:

['1    0000 :                                ', '2    0100 :                  org $100      ', '3    0100 : start:                         ', '4    0100 :         A9 10    lda #$10      ', '5    0102 :         A2 00    ldx #$00      ', '6    0104 : loop:                          ', '7    0104 :         9D 00 10 sta $1000,x   ', '8    0107 :         E8       inx           ', '9    0108 :         E9 01    sbc #$01      ', '10   010A :         10 F8    bpl loop      ', '11   010C :         60       rts           ']

The Symbol Table
----------------

You can also see the symbol table as a dictionary after assembling:
    >>> a.symbols
    {'start': 256, 'loop': 260}

The Object Code Map
-------------------

Finally, you can see the list of object code values, but in decimal, since that's how python displays by default:
        >>> a.object_code[256:269]
        [169, 16, 162, 0, 157, 0, 16, 232, 233, 1, 16, 248, 96]
        >>>

The assembler keeps a complete map of the 64K memory space of the 6502 and populates the code and values into that map. The 'object_code' class variable is a list containing the map. Each untouched location is set to -1. Other values indicate the 8 bit value at that location.

After assembling the code into the map, it is possible to add in other things to the map by assigning to the object_code list. E.G.

        a.object_code[0xfffd] = 0x00
        a.object_code[0xfffc] = 0x10
Which would set the reset vector to 0x1000.

Pseudo-ops and Directives
-------------------------

; Comment
ORG address - Set the current assembly location
EQU - Define a label and its value (see "Labels" below)
DB - Generate 8-bit values
DW - Generate 16-bit values
DDW - Generate 32-bit values
DQW - Generate 64-bit values
LE - For multi word data (DW, DDW and DQW) set the encoding to little endian
BE - For multi word data (DW, DDW and DQW) set the encoding to big endian
The assembler defaults to little endian.

DB, DW, DDW and DQW all work in the same way:

* The argument is one or more comma-separated *items*
* Each *item* is one of
  * Decimal number
  * Hex number (indicated by $ prefix)
  * Octal number (indicated by @ prefix)
  * Binary number (indicated by % prefix)
  * Label (the & prefix is accepted but optional)
  * String (delimited "thus")
  * An expression combining numbers and labels with + and -, optionally
    prefixed with < (low byte) or > (high byte) - see "Expressions" below
* Each string *item* is transformed into one 8-bit *value* per character (the ASCII code of the character)
* Every other item represents a single *value*
* Every *value* is zero-padded or truncated to generate one or more *bytes* in the object code (1 byte-per-value for DB, 2 for DW etc.)
* The assembler generates a warning when a *value* is truncated

Examples:

DB $0d, "the rain in spain", $0
DB entry, loop                   ; both truncated to low byte
DW entry, "fish"                 ; each character padded to 16-bits
DW jumptable+4                   ; label arithmetic
DB <entry, >entry                ; low byte, high byte

Prefixes
--------

The prefixes $, @, % can also be used with numeric arguments to instructions

Labels
------

A word followed by a colon makes a label. It can be on its own line, or in front of an instruction or directive. Examples:

              ORG $100
alabel:                 ; A label on its own - value is $100 because of previous ORG
              NOP       ; 1 byte op-code
anotherlabel: STA #$10  ; A label with an instruction - value is $101
yalabel:      EQU $1234 ; A label with a value - value is $1234
loop:         STA #$20  ; A label with an instruction - value is $103 because "STA #$10" occupies 2 bytes

An EQU directive explicitly declares the value of a label. A label without an EQU takes the implicit address where it occurs. All EQU directives must be resolved in pass1. A consequence of this is that the value of an EQU can be a backward symbolic reference
but cannot be a forward symbolic reference.

Any address or 16 bit data field can be replaced with a declared label and the label address will be inserted there.
In DB/DW/DDW/DQW declarations a label can be used directly; the & prefix is accepted for backward compatibility but is optional. Examples:

        dw  $1000, @2000, 123  ; Implicit numbers have a base prefix.
ttable: dw  l1, l2, l3         ; labels in a DW
        dw  &l1, &l2, &l3      ; the same, with the optional & prefix
        org $1000
l1:     lda #$20
        jmp skip
l2:     lda #$30
        jmp skip
l3:     lda #$40
skip:   sta $10

Expressions
-----------

Wherever a number or label is accepted (instruction operands, DB/DW/DDW/DQW items, ORG and EQU values) you can use a simple expression instead:

* Terms are numbers in any base ($ hex, @ octal, % binary, decimal) or labels
* Terms can be added and subtracted with + and -
* The whole expression can be prefixed with < to take the low byte or > to take the high byte of its value

Examples:

        sta dp+1        ; the byte after dp
        lda #<h_last    ; low byte of the address of h_last
        lda #>h_last    ; high byte of the address of h_last
        lda buffer+2,x  ; indexing works with expressions too
        dw  vector-1    ; expressions in data declarations
        db  <entry+3    ; low byte of (entry + 3)

Note there is no operator precedence or bracketing; expressions are evaluated left to right with + and - only.

Assembling Into the Same Map
----------------------------

You can call the assembler() class method multiple times; by default, the object_code map is retained between calls. This allows you to assemble multiple pieces of code into different locations and they will be added to the map.
The print_object_code() class method displays the current object code map.
E.G. The following code assembles a sequence, then modifies its origin, then reassembles it:
        from asm6502 import asm6502
        a = asm6502()
        lines = [' ORG $1000', ' NOP', ' LDA #$20', 'here: NOP', ' DB 10,11,12,13', ' RTS']
        a.assemble(lines)
        lines[0] = ' ORG $2000'
        a.assemble(lines)
        a.print_object_code()

This yields this memory map with the same code in two places.
        >>> a.print_object_code()
        OBJECT CODE
        *
        1000: EA A9 20 EA 0A 0B 0C 0D 60
        *
        2000: EA A9 20 EA 0A 0B 0C 0D 60
        *

The default behaviour of the assemble() class method is set by variables that have default values:

        a.assemble(lines, clear_lst=True, clear_sym=True, clear_obj=False)

Setting clear_sym=False retains the symbol table from the previous call, and setting clear_lst=False allows multiple pieces of source code to be grouped together.

Setting clear_sym=True also allows you to establish symbols prior to running the assembler, then reference them in the code:

        from asm6502 import asm6502
        a = asm6502()
        lines = [' ORG $1000', ' NOP', ' LDA #$20', ' JMP syblue', 'here: NOP', ' RTS']
        a.symbols['skyblue'] = 0x4500
        a.assemble(lines, clear_sym=FALSE)

Getting hex dump format data in and out
---------------------------------------
After assembling you can output the object code as a hex dump with * marking the unpopulated spaces

        >>> a.print_object_code()
        >>> a.print_object_code(canonical=True)

The second version used unix hexdump format, which includes an ASCII decode of printable characters.

An optional offset can be used to affect the address field in the output. For example, to generate data for a PROM programmer that expects the addresses to be relative to the first location in the ROM, choose an offset that causes the start address to wrap back to 0 like this:

        >>> a.print_object_code(canonical=True, offset=-0xb400)

You can also load the object code map from a file in hexdump format, also with an optional offset:

        >>> a.load_object_code("some_file.txt", offset=0x400)


Getting IntelHex format data out
--------------------------------
After assembling you can output the object code in intelhex format.
calling the intelhex() method returns lines of intelhex as a list.

        >>> a.intelhex()
        [':10010000A000B90000990020B90001990021B900', ':1001100002990022B90003990023B90004990024', ':10012000B90005990025B90006B90026B9000799', ':0E0130000027B90008990028C8D0D04C59FF', ':10100000A000B90000990020C8D0D0A900850085', ':1010100002A9018501A9218503B2009202E602E6', ':1010200000D0F8E603E601A501C909D0EE4C59FF', ':00000001FF']
        
Calling the print_intelhex() method outputs intelhex format object code to stdout.        
        >>> a.print_intelhex()
        :10010000A000B90000990020B90001990021B900
        :1001100002990022B90003990023B90004990024
        :10012000B90005990025B90006B90026B9000799
        :0E0130000027B90008990028C8D0D04C59FF
        :10100000A000B90000990020C8D0D0A900850085
        :1010100002A9018501A9218503B2009202E602E6
        :1010200000D0F8E603E601A501C909D0EE4C59FF
        :00000001FF
        >>> 

Getting SRecord format data out
--------------------------------
After assembling you can output the object code in S19 Srecord format.
calling the srecord() method returns lines of S19 S Record as a list.

The parameters are (int:version, int:revision, str:module name, str:comment)

>>> a.srecords(10,20,"Module Name,","Comment")
['S02e00000a144d6f64756c65204e616d652c436f6d6d656e74ad', 'S12e1000600D0C0B0AEA20A9EA96', 'S12e2000600D0C0B0AEA20A9EA86', 'S5030003f9', 'S9032008d4']

Calling the print_srecords() method outputs S19 format object code to stdout.        
>>> a.print_srecords(10,20,"Module Name,","Comment")
S02e00000a144d6f64756c65204e616d652c436f6d6d656e74ad
S12e1000600D0C0B0AEA20A9EA96
S12e2000600D0C0B0AEA20A9EA86
S5030003f9
S9032008d4

The Simulator and Disassembler
------------------------------

#The simulator is in sim6502.py, the disassembler is in dis6502.py
#So start with all three..
import asm6502
import sim6502
import dis6502

# The assembler code
src = """
<assembly goes here>
"""
lines = src.splitlines()

#The simulator must be given an object code map. You can get it from the assembler:

# Assemble the code in a list called lines.
a = asm6502.asm6502(debug=0)
a.assemble(lines)
object_code = a.object_code[:]

# Then instantiate the simulator.
# Also pass it the symbol table so it can know addresses
s = sim6502.sim6502(object_code, symbols=a.symbols)

# And instantiate the disassembler:
d = dis6502.dis6502(object_code, symbols=a.symbols)

# Now
# s.reset() will reset the simulation
# s.execute() will execute the current instruction
# The 6502 state will be in
#   s.pc  Program Counter
#   s.a   Accumulator
#   s.x   X registers
#   s.y   Y register
#   s.sp  stack pointer
#   s.cc  Flags
# d.disassemble(address) will disassemble the instruction as the address and
#                        will return a text string of the disassembly
#
# E.G.

s.reset()

print
print "SIMULATION START"
print
# Print a header for the simulator/disassembler output
print ("LABEL      " + "ADDR HEX      INSTR").ljust(status_indent)+" PC   A  X  Y  SP   Status"

# Print the initial state
print " ".ljust(status_indent) + " %04x %02x %02x %02x %04x %02x" % (s.pc,s.a,s.x,s.y,s.sp,s.cc)

# Execute 200 instructions
for i in xrange(200):
    # Disassemble the current instruction
    distxt = d.disassemble_line(s.pc)

    # Execute that instruction
    s.execute()

    # Print out the disassembled instruction followed by the simulator state
    print distxt.ljust(status_indent) + " %04x %02x %02x %02x %04x %02x" % (s.pc,s.a,s.x,s.y,s.sp,s.cc)

# Each output line will then show the address, the hex, the instruction executed and the state of the 6502 after the execution.


The Disassembler for code exploration
-------------------------------------

You can also use the disassembler for code exploration: iteratively disassembling code and then annotating labels. For example consider a file tiny.hexdump with this content:

00000100  a9 10 a2 00 9d 00 10 e8  e9 01 10 f8 60           |............`|

Now try this (see small_dis_example.py):

..
from asm6502 import asm6502
from dis6502 import dis6502

a = asm6502() # only so we can use the loader..
a.load_object_code("tiny.hexdump")

d = dis6502(a.object_code, a.symbols) # a.symbols is empty

z = d.disassemble_region(0x100, 13)
for line in list(z):
    print (line)

The call to disassemble_region() returns a generator, list() consumes its output and the 'for' loop prints it. The result looks like this:

           0100 a9 10    lda  #$10
           0102 a2 00    ldx  #$00
           0104 9d 00 10 sta  $1000,x
           0107 e8       inx  
           0108 e9 01    sbc  #$01
           010a 10 f8    bpl  $f8 ; $0104
           010c 60       rts  

Observe that there is a loop that branches to $f8 which is backwards; the helpful comment shows that the destination address is $104. Add entries to the symbol table for the entry point of the code and another for the loop destination. Whenever you manipulate the symbol table you need to call build_symbols_xref() to rebuild an internal data structure:

d.symbols['start'] = 0x100
d.symbols['loop'] = 0x104
d.build_symbols_xref()

Call disassemble_region() again as before and you will see the labels annotated into the output:

start:     0100 a9 10    lda  #$10
           0102 a2 00    ldx  #$00
loop:      0104 9d 00 10 sta  $1000,x
           0107 e8       inx  
           0108 e9 01    sbc  #$01
           010a 10 f8    bpl  loop ; $0104
           010c 60       rts  

The final trick is that the disassembler will create labels for you. You must call it twice, setting the gen_symbols argument to True. On the first call it populates the symbol table. On the second call, it annotates the symbols onto the output. Like this:

z = d.disassemble_region(0x100, 13, gen_symbols=True)
list(z)
# Build data structure
d.build_symbols_xref()
# Pass 2: and output..
z = d.disassemble_region(0x100, 13)
for line in list(z):
    print (line)

The first "list(z)" might need some explanation: because disassemble_region is a generator, it does not actually perform the calls until it is enumerated (which is done here using 'list'). The output looks like this:

           0100 a9 10    lda  #$10
           0102 a2 00    ldx  #$00
L0104:     0104 9d 00 10 sta  L1000,x
           0107 e8       inx  
           0108 e9 01    sbc  #$01
           010a 10 f8    bpl  L0104 ; $0104
           010c 60       rts  

A symbol is generated for any referenced address, provided one doesn't currently exist. This includes references outside the region being disassembled (L1000 in this example). You can mix this technique with manual manipulation of the symbol table. For example, as an iterative process of exploring a piece of unknown code.

Assembling From the Command Line
--------------------------------
The normal way to assemble code using this library is to write a python program to feed
the assembly file lines to the assembler then use the output as required.

If you want a more normal approach of using the command line to assemble a file, the
6502asm program will do that.

usage: 6502asm [-h] [-l LISTING_FILENAME] [-i IHEX_FILENAME] [-s SYMBOL_FILENAME] [-v]
               [filename]

Assembles a 6502 .asm file using py6502

positional arguments:
  filename              6502 Assembler source file .asm by default. Omit for stdin

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -l, --list LISTING_FILENAME
                        Filename to send listing output to. Defaults to <filename>.lst
  -i, --intelhex IHEX_FILENAME
                        Filename to send intelhex output to. Defaults to <filename>.hex
  -s, --symbol SYMBOL_FILENAME
                        Filename to send symbol table output to. Defaults to <filename>.sym
  -v, --verbose

Typical use is to feed it an assembler filename ending in .asm. It will create output 
files with the filename, replacing .asm with .lst, hex and .sym for the listing, the
intelhex output and the symbol table files.

E.G.

> 6502asm maze_10print.asm
Assembling from file: maze_10print.asm
Listing writing to:  maze_10print.lst
Symbol table written to:  maze_10print.sym
Intel Hex object code written to:  maze_10print.hex

If the output files already exist, it will create unique output filenames by incrementing
a counter in the filename.

E.G. maze_10print.lst leads to maze_10print(1).lst which leads to maze_10print(2).lst
and so on.

Making asm6502, dis6502 and sim6502 available in externally managed environments
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

To make the python libraries available outside the source directory can be done
with pip.

> git clone https://github.com/dj-on-github/py6502
> cd py6502
> pip install .

However this won't work in many situations because the system installed python
is "externally managed". 

The method that works for me is to pass --user (to install in my user file area) and
--break-system-packages to get it to add them there even though the python being
used is externally managed.

> git clone https://github.com/dj-on-github/py6502
> cd py6502
> python3 -m pip install --user --break-system-packages .

And to get the command line 6502asm program available for the local user:
> cp src/6502asm ~/bin

or for site wide, put it whereever system wide binaries go.

# Retrolarium Disassembler

Retrolarium Disassembler turns a ROM image into a complete, modular source
project that rebuilds byte for byte. The NES pipeline turns a profiled iNES
image into a ca65 project; mapper profiles describe the physical-to-logical
projections used for independent bank analysis and source emission. Analysis
runs headless Ghidra with pinned versions plus the disassembler's own passes,
and the result is always verified against the original image.

The Mega Drive pipeline parses cartridge headers and checksums, analyzes the
68000 and statically recovered Z80 payloads as independent Ghidra Programs,
emits a complete modular AS (asl) project, and proves an exact rebuild. Stable
symbols, big-endian/relative pointer candidates and cross-CPU copy evidence are
published through a versioned project manifest.

The SNES pipeline now reaches the same integration boundary. Its versioned image
component parses plain LoROM/HiROM containers, optional copier headers, mirrored
checksums, native/emulation vectors and ROM/WRAM/SRAM bus windows. A
project-owned ca65 probe builds the same W65C816 state and pointer cases as both
LoROM and HiROM. Statically proven APU uploads are extracted and analyzed as
independent SPC700 Programs; ExROM layouts and enhancement chips are rejected in
v1.

The generated source is deliberately conservative: Ghidra-recognized official
6502 instructions become assembly, accepted pointer tables and interrupt vectors
become symbolic entries, and every unclassified or unsupported byte remains
explicit `.byte` data. The iNES header, trainer and CHR payload are separate
binary assets. A whole-ROM `.incbin` fallback is never used.

The disassembler builds on `retrolarium-core` only (container parsers, the
disassembly manifest contract). Generated projects are built, verified and
launched by [Retrolarium Kit](https://github.com/Retrolarium/retrolarium-kit)
(`rltool project ...`), whose bundled assemblers need no Docker.
`rldisasm preset`, which turns a recognized game into a ready-to-open Studio
project, is the one command that needs the kit installed
(`retrolarium-disassembler[studio]`).

## Layout

```text
src/retrolarium_disassembler/
  cli.py            rldisasm; every command imports what it runs
  preset.py         ROM -> Studio project (the only module that imports the kit)
  facts.py          neutral instruction facts shared by every CPU
  benchmark.py      pointer-table scoring against an isolated oracle
  toolchain.py      pinned Ghidra + language installs (toolchains/*.lock.json)
  ghidra/           headless Ghidra bridge and its Java scripts (scripts/)
  nes/              iNES bank analysis, pointers, ca65 emitter
  megadrive/        68000 + Z80 pipeline, AS (asl) emitter, pointers, symbols
  m68k/             68000 passes: dispatch/, callbacks/, frames/, records/, repair/
  z80/              Z80 dispatch tables
  snes/             W65C816 analysis, SPC700 uploads, ca65 emitter
tests/              python -m unittest discover -s tests; folders mirror the
                    package, scripts/ covers tools/, builders.py files hold
                    the shared test images and facts
tools/              python -m tools.<group>.<name>, from this folder:
  references/       preparing the reference disassemblies (evaluation only)
  benchmarks/       scoring ROM-only disassembly against them
  reports/          HTML and Markdown source comparisons
  compiler_scan/    compiler traces in ROM sets
fixtures/           open test games, synthetic probes and their Docker images
docs/               pipeline contracts, corpus baselines and reviews
```

## Current NES boundary

- iNES 1.0 containers;
- inspect/projection profiles for mapper 0 (NROM), 3 (CNROM) and 66
  (GNROM/GxROM);
- independent headless analysis of every canonical PRG bank through generated
  mapper-0 views, with bank-qualified neutral instruction facts;
- exact disassembly and rebuild for mapper 0, 3 and 66;
- headless Ghidra 12.1.3 plus GhidraNes v20260531;
- complete physical PRG coverage and overlap checks;
- stable technical labels for functions and control-flow targets;
- explainable `u16le` and adjacent split-low/high pointer candidates;
- conservative pointer promotion with evidence, contradictions and overlap
  checks;
- exact ca65/ld65 rebuild verification in the fixture Docker image.

NES 2.0 and unprofiled mappers are rejected explicitly. Overlapping PRG windows
are analyzed independently and emitted as ordered ca65 segments with
bank-qualified symbols.

## Quick start

Run the source-checkout launcher from the repository root. Python 3.11+, Java 21
and Docker are required for the complete verified path.

```powershell
python fixtures/scripts/build_fixtures.py toolchain nes
python fixtures/scripts/build_fixtures.py build `
  nes.honkeypong nes.rhde nes.cnrom_probe nes.gnrom_probe
python rldisasm.py ghidra install
python rldisasm.py nes disassemble `
  fixtures/nes/bin/HonkeyPong.nes `
  --output build/honkey-disassembly
rltool project build `
  build/honkey-disassembly/manifest.json
rltool project verify `
  build/honkey-disassembly/manifest.json
```

`ghidra install` downloads the versions recorded in
`src/retrolarium_disassembler/toolchains/disassembly.lock.json`, verifies the
archive sizes and SHA-256 values, rejects unsafe ZIP members and installs into
the ignored `.tools/` directory. An existing compatible install can be selected
with `--ghidra-home` or `RETROLARIUM_GHIDRA_HOME`. The same command installs the
pinned MIT W65C816 and SPC700 languages as `Retrolarium65816` and
`RetrolariumSPC700`, compiles them with Ghidra's SLEIGH compiler and preserves
their upstream licenses; it does not install the upstream SNES cartridge loader.

### Mega Drive / Genesis

```powershell
python fixtures/scripts/build_fixtures.py toolchain megadrive
python fixtures/scripts/build_fixtures.py build `
  megadrive.dualcpu_probe megadrive.5stars megadrive.dragons_castle `
  megadrive.miniplanets
python rldisasm.py megadrive disassemble `
  fixtures/megadrive/bin/megadrive-dualcpu-probe.bin `
  --output build/megadrive-disassembly
rltool project build `
  build/megadrive-disassembly/retrolarium-project.json
rltool project verify `
  build/megadrive-disassembly/retrolarium-project.json
rltool project launch `
  build/megadrive-disassembly/retrolarium-project.json `
  --mame path/to/mame.exe --machine genesis --seconds 2
```

Mega Drive source is emitted below `generated/src/`, with `main.s` as the
address-ordered translation-unit index, `.s` files for the 68000, `data/` for
binary inputs, and technical work-RAM/hardware definitions under `src/memory/`.
Proven Z80 uploads also produce rebuildable `src/sound/z80/programNN.asm` units;
`project build` assembles them before the 68000 ROM. ROM-derived instructions
with supported operand forms are emitted as mnemonics; the remaining recognized
instructions retain their original bytes and disassembly comments.
`project verify` checks the rebuilt ROM against the input byte for byte.
Generated `loc_`, `sub_`, `tbl_`, and `off_` symbols use IDA-style lower-case
prefixes. Long `$FF` padding runs use `org` and are counted separately as
`padding_bytes` in the project coverage report. Technical references whose
targets fall inside such a run are suppressed, so immediate constants mistaken
for data addresses cannot split one padding range into artificial tables.
Unclassified ROM spans of at least 256 bytes are emitted as `data/opaque-*.bin`
files when they contain no analyzed instructions, accepted pointer tables,
existing assets, or internal technical symbols. A later analysis result
automatically splits an opaque include when it finds code or structure inside
it.

The Mega Drive analysis builds its complete decoder seed plan in Python. The
first pass validates cartridge vectors, ROM-to-RAM code-copy loops, PC-indexed
`bra.s`/`bra.w` and dense `bra.w` dispatch tables, and counted RAM trampoline
builders. It then runs a Python abstract interpreter over the known 68000
control-flow graph. The interpreter propagates constants, small value sets,
ranges, registers, flags, and selected memory writes, then feeds proven indirect
branch targets back to Ghidra for decoding. Analysis repeats until no new
targets, inline-data bounds, decode requests or instruction repairs are found. A
32-pass safety limit fails the operation instead of emitting a partially applied
seed plan. `analysis/m68k/abstract-analysis.json` records each seed's kind,
confidence, and evidence together with reached states, indirect edges, widening
points, unresolved jumps, RAM handler candidates, and packed orphan candidates.
`analysis/m68k/python-seeds.txt` is the decoder entry-point plan. Speculative
decode requests and canonical boundary repairs have separate plans and never
become independent roots. The Ghidra pre-script labels cartridge vectors and
applies the seed plan; it does not discover targets. Packed orphan recovery only
considers short gaps between known instructions after a terminal flow, rejects
existing data/read targets, and requires either a compact gap or a return opcode
before known code resumes. After convergence, the Kit retains backend-decoded
instructions only when they are reachable from a cartridge vector, direct call,
proven decoder seed, proven indirect target, or an accepted structural code-use
hypothesis. A backend function label alone is insufficient. This removes
isolated instruction-shaped data without using reference source. The discarded
addresses are recorded in `analysis/m68k/abstract-analysis.json`. The bounded
probe and repair protocols record their protections and audit files beside it.
The interpreter updates `X/N/Z/V/C` for modeled move, logical, arithmetic,
compare, test, and bit-test operations. It records each conditional branch as
true, false, or unknown in the abstract report while retaining both CFG edges;
known flags therefore add evidence without hiding alternate game states.

Generic pointer scans are advisory until code or data references the table
start. Unreferenced sequences whose values merely happen to land on instruction
starts remain `candidate` entries in `analysis/pointers.json` and are emitted as
raw data. Schema-proven structures such as cartridge vectors and counted RAM
trampoline tables can be accepted without that reference. Referenced `u32be`
arrays are also accepted as data-pointer tables when code reads them with an
indexed `move.l` and every entry points forward beyond the table. References to
aligned addresses inside one scanned run split it into the separate tables
actually selected by the program. Numeric longword tables whose values precede
the table remain candidates.

Counted animation layouts are recovered through their complete data path. The
analysis requires a proven ROM-to-work-RAM copy loop, the shared animation
reader that indexes a longword sequence table and then reads a sign-extended
word at `2(sequence,index)`, and a root stored into the same object field. Each
sequence header supplies its entry count, so the emitter can write every frame
as `dc.w target-copy_source` even though one runtime update reads only one
frame. This schema also follows animation roots selected by an outer indexed
longword table.

The standard Mega Drive startup stream is recovered as a mixed-width structure
when the loader addresses it through `a5`, consumes the canonical `movem`
fields, copies the VDP, Z80, CRAM, VSRAM and PSG portions with the matching
counted loops, and branches to the byte immediately after the block. The emitter
writes its scalar fields as `dc.w`/`dc.l`, uses generated hardware symbols for
the five device addresses, and preserves the embedded byte streams as `dc.b`.

Calls whose handler consumes variable-length inline operands, such as a software
floating-point runtime reached by `JSR` followed by an op word and optional
immediates, are proven per call site by a partial 68000 emulator. ROM bytes are
concrete, registers and RAM are unknown with per-bit tracking of data registers,
the stack is symbolic, and both successors of an unknown condition are explored
with context-sensitive joins. A site is accepted only when every explored return
lands on one even address at most 32 bytes after the call; the operands become
data and the continuation a decoder seed. Direct flow from each continuation is
walked in the same pass, so a chain of such calls resolves without one decoder
pass per call.

Compiler switches that double a long index (`ADD.L Dn,Dn`,
`MOVE.W (T,PC,Dn.L),Dn`, `JMP (T,PC,Dn.W)`) are recovered as
`megadrive.s16be.target-table_base` tables. Ghidra's element references from the
inferred index no longer split such tables, and backend switch flows of both
PC-relative and `MOVEA.W`/`ADDA.L`/`JMP (An)` word tables are bounded by the
structural table when decoded code starts right after it, so over-read entries
cannot become trusted code. Speculative packed-gap decoding treats an address
loaded by `MOVEA.L #addr,An` or `LEA addr.l,An` as data when memory is read
through that register, locally or in a direct callee; stored or jumped-through
pointers may be callbacks and are not counted. `LEA d16(PC),An` naming the
instruction right after an unconditional branch, whose callee jumps through the
same register, is a hand-made return address and seeds that continuation. Packed
orphan entries skip longword alignment padding or a NUL-terminated literal only
when a `LINK` or `MOVEM.L ...,-(SP)` prologue follows.

The Z80 analysis follows word dispatch tables when executable code loads their
address into HL, calls a recognized A-indexed word lookup through RST, and jumps
through HL. A preceding `sub` bounds the selector range. The analyzer marks the
words as data and seeds their targets in Ghidra, repeating this pass when a
newly decoded handler reveals another table. Each table and its evidence are
recorded in `analysis/z80/programNN/dispatch-tables.json`. On the Flicky ROM,
this recovers the 4-entry sound-command table and the adjacent 32- and 8-entry
coordination tables.

For an independent Flicky source benchmark, run this after disassembly:

```powershell
python -m tools.benchmarks.source `
  --reference path\to\flicky_src `
  --generated build/megadrive-disassembly/generated `
  --output build/flicky-benchmark `
  --minimum-m68k-instruction-match 99 `
  --minimum-m68k-precision 99 `
  --minimum-m68k-f1 99 `
  --minimum-m68k-source-match 99 `
  --minimum-z80-instruction-match 99 `
  --minimum-z80-precision 99 `
  --minimum-z80-f1 99 `
  --minimum-z80-source-match 97
```

This creates flattened `reference/main.s` and `generated/main.s`, source maps,
and `comparison.json`. When the reference AS listing exists, the report compares
68000 instruction addresses and encodings. If the reference Z80 driver listing
is available at `comparison/reference/z80_driver.lst`, it also compares Z80
instruction addresses and full instruction bytes. Run `project build` before
this command: the benchmark reads its 68000 and Z80 assembler listings to count
instructions actually written as mnemonics. The processor-specific minimum flags
enforce separate 68000 and Z80 targets. The legacy `--minimum-instruction-match`
and `--minimum-source-match` flags apply one threshold to both processors. The
benchmark reads the reference only after the ROM pipeline completes; no
reference source or symbols enter generation.

The instruction comparison records recall, precision, and F1 independently.
Precision counts speculative instruction starts that are absent from the
reference as false positives, so broader code recovery cannot improve the gate
by decoding arbitrary data.

In the current Flicky benchmark, the 68000 instruction analysis matches
5707/5707 reference instructions; the Z80 analysis matches 1679/1683 (99.76%
recall, 99.29% precision). The generated Z80 source emits 1646/1683 reference
instructions as mnemonics (97.8%). The assembled ROM is byte exact.

For additional independent games, the Sonic Retro reference corpus is pinned in
`tools/references/sonic.lock.json`. `tools/references/prepare_sonic.py` exports
unified assembly units, preserves build profiles, and verifies them against
upstream builds and original ROMs. The references are evaluation inputs only;
they never seed the ROM analyzer.

The Sonic disassembly benchmark (`tools/benchmarks/sonic_corpus.py`) runs
ROM-only analysis against those verified references, measures opcode recall and
precision, verifies exact rebuilds, and produces differences-only HTML.

For side-by-side editing, export the two ROM-aligned reference files after
disassembly:

```powershell
python -m tools.reports.export_flicky_reference `
  --reference path\to\flicky_src `
  --generated path\to\flicky_src_kit_test\project\generated
```

This writes `rom-000200.reference.s` and `rom-010000.reference.s` beside the
generated `rom-*.s` files. They concatenate the matching source modules from
`flicky_src/src/main.s`; the first starts at `Sys_ErrorTrap` ($000200), after
the cartridge vectors and header. These comparison files are not assembled.

For a standalone address-aligned HTML view, build both projects and run:

```powershell
python -m tools.reports.flicky_html_diff `
  --reference path\to\flicky_src `
  --generated path\to\flicky_src_kit_test\project\generated `
  --output path\to\flicky_src_kit_test\comparison\flicky-source-diff.html
```

Add `--differences-only` and choose a separate output file to generate a compact
report containing only structural data differences, raw instruction fallbacks,
and source lines present on one side of the comparison.

The page places lines from both assembler listings side by side at their ROM
addresses, with filters for source differences and instructions still emitted as
`dc.b`. Instructions with the same mnemonic and encoded bytes are treated as
equal even when their labels, symbolic operands, or size spelling differ.
Reference data rows covered by an exact generated `binclude` are also treated as
equal; reference instructions inside such a span remain visible as missing
analysis. It requires the rebuilt ROM to match the reference byte for byte.

For an actionable text and JSON report of the same build, run:

```powershell
python -m tools.reports.flicky_diff_report `
  --reference path\to\flicky_src `
  --generated path\to\flicky_src_kit_test\project\generated `
  --output path\to\flicky_src_kit_test\comparison
```

`flicky-diff.md` groups the remaining raw instruction fallbacks by mnemonic;
`flicky-diff.json` records every mismatch with its ROM address, both source
lines, bytes, and Ghidra fact. It separates missing analysis from unsupported
emission and differences limited to names or formatting.

To turn the source differences into contiguous regions for heuristic work, run:

```powershell
python -m tools.reports.flicky_discrepancy_groups `
  --reference path\to\flicky_src `
  --generated path\to\flicky_src_kit_test\project\generated `
  --output path\to\flicky_src_kit_test\comparison
```

The command writes `flicky-discrepancy-groups.md` and JSON. It removes line
wrapping noise and classifies every differing ROM interval as text, word or long
data, an opaque or missing binary include, a false pointer table, false code, or
padding. It also groups consecutive missed and extra Z80 instructions. Each M68K
group links to the matching row in the HTML report.

### SNES / Super Famicom foundation

```powershell
python fixtures/scripts/build_fixtures.py build `
  snes.lorom_probe snes.hirom_probe
python rldisasm.py snes inspect `
  fixtures/snes/bin/snes-lorom-probe.sfc
python rldisasm.py snes analyze `
  fixtures/snes/bin/snes-lorom-probe.sfc `
  --output build/snes-lorom-analysis
python rldisasm.py snes disassemble `
  fixtures/snes/bin/snes-lorom-probe.sfc `
  --output build/snes-lorom-disassembly
rltool project build `
  build/snes-lorom-disassembly/retrolarium-project.json
rltool project verify `
  build/snes-lorom-disassembly/retrolarium-project.json
```

Inspection and independent state-aware W65C816 decoding are available. Full
analysis writes evidence-bearing pointer, stable-symbol and cross-CPU reports.
The modular ca65 emitter has exact rebuild proof for both synthetic mappings and
two open-game holdouts. The strict project schema, Qt 5.15 importer and common
build/verify/MAME operations are complete. MAME's SNES driver needs the
`spc700.rom` device ROM in its ROM path; it is not distributed here. See
[`snes_image.md`](docs/snes_image.md) and
[`snes_disassembly.md`](docs/snes_disassembly.md).

The output directory contains:

```text
analysis/instructions.json              merged bank-qualified neutral facts
analysis/pointers.json                  candidates, evidence and schema registry
analysis/banks/bankNN/analysis-input.nes exact analysis projection
analysis/banks/bankNN/instructions.tsv  backend facts for one PRG bank
analysis/banks/bankNN/program.json      backend metadata for one PRG bank
analysis/banks/bankNN/headless.log      reproducible analysis log
generated/main.asm                      container and asset assembly
generated/src/prg.asm                   single-bank full-coverage PRG source
generated/src/prg-bankNN.asm            multi-bank full-coverage PRG sources
generated/assets/                       header, optional trainer and CHR
generated/linker.cfg                    exact ordered memory layout
generated/Makefile                      ca65/ld65 rebuild recipe
generated/emission.json                 source coverage statistics
generated/symbols.json                  bank-qualified integration symbols
generated/build/rebuilt.nes             rebuilt image after project build
manifest.json                           input, backend, coverage and verification result
```

All of these are reproducible build artifacts and should stay below an ignored
`build/` directory.

## Other commands

```powershell
python rldisasm.py nes inspect game.nes
python rldisasm.py nes analyze game.nes `
  --output build/game-analysis
python rldisasm.py ghidra status
python rldisasm.py verify original.nes rebuilt.nes
python rldisasm.py benchmark pointers `
  build/honkey-disassembly/analysis/pointers.json `
  fixtures/oracles/nes.honkeypong.pointer-tables.json
python rldisasm.py preset game.nes --output build/game-studio
python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

`nes analyze` writes one isolated `banks/bankNN/` workspace per canonical PRG
projection plus a merged `instructions.json`. Every instruction and flow has an
explicit bank context, while `physical_offset` remains unique across the source
ROM. For mappers not understood by GhidraNes directly, the workspace records the
exact generated mapper-0 analysis input and its SHA-256.

The versioned manifest contracts consumed by the Studio and the kit are
[`nes_disassembly.md`](docs/nes_disassembly.md),
[`megadrive_disassembly.md`](docs/megadrive_disassembly.md) and
[`snes_disassembly.md`](docs/snes_disassembly.md).

## Trust boundary

The ROM is immutable input. Ghidra is an analysis backend, not the source of
truth: its exported facts must map to the original PRG bytes without overlap.
The emitter owns every physical byte exactly once, and the final verifier
compares both size and content. Difficult control flow, such as a branch into
the interior of another decoded instruction, is preserved with a relocatable
relative expression and recorded as a diagnostic.

Oracle metadata is never an analyzer input. The separate benchmark command first
checks that the report and oracle name the same ROM hash, then measures accepted
table ranges and decoded targets. The current HonkeyPong development baseline
has precision 1.0 and recall 1.0 across four tables. Besides compact monotonic
tables, it exercises two generic evidence patterns: pointer fields in a record
reached from an accepted table, and two interleaved monotonic lanes. RHDE
remains a source-isolated holdout and retains exact rebuild verification.

## Checks before a commit

`make hooks`, once per clone, makes Git check every commit and push for stop
words and run `make lint` and `make format-check` first (see Retrolarium Core's
README, "Stop words and Git hooks"). The hooks and the Makefile use the
`retrolarium-core` checkout beside this one.

djayuffe-sid-to-json-converter-readme-md.text:
# SID to JSON Converter

An offline Commodore 64 SID analysis tool with a browser UI and command-line interface. It loads PSID/RSID files, executes supported player code with a compact 6510/C64 runtime, records SID register and voice state frame-by-frame, exports the capture as JSON, and can turn a compatible JSON capture into Standard MIDI File type 1.

**Release:** v1.0.0 · **License:** GPL-3.0-or-later · **Copyright:** © 2026 Ulf Bertilsson

> The browser workflow runs locally. It does not upload SID or JSON files, and it does not require an API key or network connection after dependencies are installed.

## Features

- PSID and RSID header parsing with strict size, song-range, load-address and C64-memory-boundary validation.
- PAL/NTSC timing selection from SID v2NG clock flags.
- In-browser 6502, CIA, VIC-II and SID state simulation for player execution.
- Frame JSON containing all 25 SID registers, voice pitch/envelope/waveform state, gate triggers, and filter state.
- JSON-to-MIDI type-1 export with conductor, voice and optional drum tracks.
- Pitch bend, ADSR/pulse/filter automation, noise-to-drum mapping, optional quantization, gap merging and arpeggio-to-chord conversion.
- Defensive JSON validation at every conversion boundary: frame ordering, register ranges, voice/filter values and capture duration must be internally consistent.
- Smart quantization evaluates straight and triplet grids, while preserving unquantized timing when there is no confident match.
- Fully bundled React/Vite/Tailwind build: no CDN, import map or API key is required at runtime.

## Supported inputs

- **SID files:** PSID and RSID versions 1–4 with a valid header, load address, subtune range, and C64-memory-sized program image.
- **JSON files:** captures produced by this converter, or compatible traces that satisfy the documented frame, register, voice, filter, and timing validation rules.
- **MIDI output:** Standard MIDI File type 1, suitable for DAWs and sequencers that accept `.mid` files.

The project intentionally does not claim support for multi-SID tunes, ROM-dependent loaders, digi/sample playback, or cycle-perfect raster behavior. See [Accuracy boundaries](#accuracy-boundaries) before relying on a conversion for archival or emulation research.

## Installation and local development

Requirements: Node.js 20+ and pnpm 10+.

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm run typecheck
pnpm run build
pnpm run verify
pnpm run dev
```

The browser build is entirely local: SID/JSON data is not uploaded and no API key is required. `pnpm run build` produces the browser bundle in `dist/` and the standalone CLI bundle in `dist-cli/`; both directories are generated and intentionally excluded from Git.

To use the CLI without the browser after building it:

```sh
node dist-cli/sid-json.mjs --help
```

### Browser quick start

1. Open the local URL printed by Vite.
2. Drop a PSID or RSID file into **SID → JSON**.
3. Set a capture limit (start with 60 seconds) and select the subtune, numbered from 1.
4. Choose **Convert to JSON**. A successful capture also prepares a MIDI download using the selected MIDI settings.
5. Download JSON for forensic/register analysis, or MIDI for a DAW sketch.

For a JSON capture produced elsewhere, use the **JSON → MIDI** panel. The browser validates the file before conversion and reports incompatible captures instead of producing a broken MIDI file.

### Choose a workflow

| Goal | Recommended command or setting |
| --- | --- |
| Inspect header and supported subtunes | `sid-json inspect tune.sid` |
| Preserve exact frame positions | `sid-json sid-to-json tune.sid --seconds 180` |
| Create a musical first-pass MIDI | `sid-json sid-to-midi tune.sid --quantize auto --note-duration smart` |
| Keep chip arpeggios as separate notes | Do not use `--arps-to-chords` |
| Turn fast arpeggios into DAW chords | Add `--arps-to-chords` |
| Treat noise as pitched material | Add `--no-drums` |

## Command-line interface

The same parser, capture runtime and MIDI writer are available without the browser UI. Build once, then run the CLI:

```sh
pnpm run build:cli
pnpm run cli -- inspect tune.sid
pnpm run cli -- sid-to-json tune.sid --seconds 180 --song 1 -o tune.json
pnpm run cli -- json-to-midi tune.json --quantize none -o tune.mid
pnpm run cli -- sid-to-midi tune.sid --json-out tune.json --quantize auto -o tune.mid
```

`sid-to-json` defaults to a 60-second capture and writes JSON alongside the source SID. `sid-to-midi` performs capture and MIDI export in one command, with optional `--json-out`. `json-to-midi` accepts `--quantize` (including `1/16T` and `1/8T` triplets), `--octave-shift`, `--min-note-frames`, `--note-duration`, `--no-expression`, `--minimal-automation`, `--no-merge-gaps`, `--no-drums`, and `--arps-to-chords`. Use `validate-json` before batch MIDI conversion. Run `pnpm run cli -- --help` for the complete reference.

`pnpm run verify` creates an isolated synthetic PSID fixture and checks malformed SID/JSON rejection, deterministic SID-to-JSON output, PAL frame timing, custom-IRQ PSID dispatch, and the complete MIDI chunk/end-marker structure.

See [the detailed usage guide](docs/USAGE.md) for copy-ready commands, output conventions, option recipes, and troubleshooting.

## Outputs and compatibility

- **JSON** is the durable analysis format. It includes parsed SID metadata and primary register/voice/filter snapshots at video-frame boundaries.
- **MIDI** is a type-1 Standard MIDI File designed for import into mainstream DAWs. It conveys inferred notes and controller automation, not SID audio.
- **Validation** is built into the browser and available through `sid-json validate-json`; use it before converting archived or third-party traces.

Generated files are never committed by default. Keep captures under a local `exports/` directory or another project-specific location.

## Release status

The current public release is [v1.0.0](https://github.com/djayuffe/sid-to-json-converter/releases/tag/v1.0.0). It is validated with TypeScript type checks, deterministic synthetic PSID/RSID captures, JSON validation, MIDI chunk checks, and a production Vite build. Report reproducible issues through the [issue tracker](https://github.com/djayuffe/sid-to-json-converter/issues), including the SID header from `sid-json inspect` and the exact command or browser setting used.

## MIDI interpretation

The MIDI export represents musical control data inferred from SID registers, not rendered SID audio. It maps frequency to notes/pitch bend, gate/envelope to note timing and velocity, pulse and filter values to controller data, and SID noise to General MIDI drum notes. Use the JSON export when you need the raw register capture for inspection or a different downstream mapping.

For the timing model, supported C64 runtime behavior, JSON fields, MIDI controller map, and practical export recipes, see [the emulation and format guide](docs/EMULATION_AND_FORMAT.md).

## Accuracy boundaries

The included runtime is a pragmatic SID-player tracer, not a transistor-level 6581/8580 audio emulator. It supports RAM banking, a minimal vector/IRQ boot environment, CIA timer IRQs, VIC raster IRQs and standard IRQ indirection for conventional player drivers. Complex loaders, ROM-dependent RSID programs, multi-SID files and cycle-perfect raster effects may require a full C64 emulator. Unsupported 6502 opcodes, non-returning init routines and over-budget PSID play calls fail explicitly rather than silently producing a partial capture.

## Project layout

```text
App.tsx                     browser workflow and export controls
services/sid/SidParser.ts   PSID/RSID validation and metadata parsing
services/sid/SidPlayer.ts   C64 execution and frame capture
services/sid/C64System.ts   CPU bus, CIA and VIC timing model
services/sid/SidChip.ts     SID register/envelope snapshot model
services/sid/JsonToMidi.ts  JSON-to-Standard-MIDI writer
services/sid/SidTypes.ts    stable JSON capture types
docs/USAGE.md               CLI recipes and troubleshooting
docs/EMULATION_AND_FORMAT.md runtime, JSON and MIDI reference
```

## Verification

Before submitting a change, run:

```sh
pnpm run typecheck
pnpm run verify
pnpm run build
```

The regression suite uses temporary synthetic PSID and RSID fixtures. It checks deterministic captures, PAL timing, PSID direct-play dispatch, CIA IRQ-driven RSID execution, malformed SID/JSON rejection, and generated MIDI chunk structure.

## License and copyright

The repository includes the complete, unmodified GNU GPL version 3 text. The `-or-later` designation permits recipients to follow GPLv3 or any later version published by the Free Software Foundation.

# oscar64

Oscar64 is a C/C++ cross compiler running on a modern system (such as a Windows PC, Mac or Linux machine) and targets the classic 6502 family of processors.  It is mainly focused on Commodore systems such as the C64, PET or VIC20.  The compiler supports C99 and many C++ features up to variadic templates and lambda functions.

The purpose of this compiler is to eliminate the need to write 6502 assembler code to achieve high code density and fast execution speed.  It continues to improve with all the games, demos and tools written by it.  It supports disk overlays and banked cartridges for larger projects.

The C64 executes 442 dhrystone V2.2 iteration per second, when compiled with Oscar64 and -O3 (which shows that the ancient dhrystone benchmark is no match to an optimizing compiler).

[Full reference manual](oscar64.md)
[Additional samples and tutorials](https://github.com/drmortalwombat/OscarTutorials)

TIImageTool

Version 3.0.8
June 2025

A tool for working with TI99 disk images 
intended for use in emulators

NICKNAME
--------

TIImageTool is sometimes referred to as TIMT.


PREREQUISITES
-------------

1. Java

You need a recent Java Runtime Environment and a JDK for building. As of 2016, 
Java is available from Oracle's web site. Alternatively, you can use
the Open Source implementation OpenJDK via

   http://openjdk.java.net/


2. Serial support (RXTX)
   
Also, to be able to compile TIImageTool, you have to put a copy of
the RXTXcomm.jar library into the ext folder. During runtime, RXTX need not
be installed; the depending features will be disabled in that case.

RXTX is available from Github (https://github.com/rxtx/rxtx).
   

3. Raw device access (CF7)

For reading from and writing to CF7 cards, raw device access is required 
which is not easily feasible for Java programs, and across different platforms.
Moreover, popular Linux distributions dropped the gksu tool for security 
reasons. 

For these reasons, I decided to drop the built-in support for reading and 
writing CF7 cards. The "dd" program ("dd.exe" for Windows) is a suitable tool
for reading and writing CF cards. Instead of calling the "dd" tool, TIImageTool
will now just suggest a command line that you have to use.

After pulling an image dump from the CF card, you can easily work with it in
TIImageTool, including adding/removing volumes, and of course working on those
volumes. Later, you have to use dd to write back the changed image.

If you do not plan to work with CF7 cards, you need not care about all this.


INSTALLING and RUNNING
----------------------

Unpack the distribution zip package. You can launch TIImageTool 

- from the command line using

     java -jar tiimagetool.jar

- from the desktop in Windows by

     double-click on tiimagetool.jar

- from the desktop in Linux/MacOS or other systems

     depends on your system configuration; make sure that the JAR 
     file type is associated with starting the Java environment.

     
DOCUMENTATION
-------------

TIImageTool contains a built-in manual that you can open with F1. Also have a look
at my website (www.mizapf.de) for updates.
     

BUGS and SUGGESTIONS
--------------------

Your feedback is welcome. Mail your comments, suggestions, or 
bug reports to ti99@mizapf.de.


LICENSING
---------

TIImageTool is freely distributable and redistributable under the
conditions of the GNU General Public License GPL v3. Please consult
the file LICENSING for details.

TI99Recv is a simple program to transfer disk images from the TI to the PC over a standard serial cable.

The raw program file, DSKXFER, is the TI side. It has an XMODEM header on it, so use XModem and a terminal program to transfer it to the TI. Use E/A#5 to start DSKXFER.

The .DSK file is a TI DSK image that includes the DSKXFER program. Note the TI Source Code is intended to be built with c99 by Clint Pulley.

On the PC, start TI99Recv. By default it puts the files in C:\NEW\TI, but since you may not have that folder, click the browse button to select a destination folder.

This is a really simple program. It runs at 19.2k, and just sends one sector at a time. It expects the disk in DSK1, and uses the RS232 device through direct hardware access. On the PC, it expects to use COM1.

The TI side has two modes:

1) Bitmap - sends only the sectors on the floppy marked as used (usually faster)

2) Full disk - sends all sectors, used or not.

You can abort the TI side by holding '~' (FCTN-W). You can quit the TI side by pressing QUIT. Neither action will harm your floppy - it's only reading.

The PC side is a standard Windows app.

Source is available for both sides. Please contact me before redistributing it or modified versions of it.

# greaseweazle-utils

Tools and a starter disk-image library for reading/writing vintage floppies
with a [Greaseweazle](https://github.com/keirf/greaseweazle).

## What's here

- **`bin/gwtool`** — a friendly CLI over Greaseweazle's `gw`. It knows the right
  disk format per machine (Amiga, C64, VIC-20, Atari, TI-99/4A, CoCo, Apple II).
- **`config/diskdefs_custom.cfg`** — extra disk formats not built into
  Greaseweazle (TI-99/4A).
- **`disk-images/`** — a curated set of disk images (public-domain/CC0,
  demoscene, user-group/homebrew), one folder per machine, each with a
  `SOURCES.txt`. See the good-faith notice under [Licensing](#licensing).
- **`bin/fetch-disk-images.py`** — (re)downloads that library.
- **`.venv/`** — Python virtualenv with Greaseweazle (git-clone install;
  Homebrew bundles its own copy).
- **[`packaging/gwtool.rb`](packaging/gwtool.rb)** + **[`PACKAGING.md`](PACKAGING.md)**
  — Homebrew formula and publish checklist.
- **[`MANUAL.md`](MANUAL.md)** — the full user manual. **Start there.**
- **[`LICENSE`](LICENSE)** — MIT (covers the tool + docs; the disk images keep
  their own status).

## Installation

You need a Greaseweazle board + a floppy drive. Pick one install mode:

### Option A — Homebrew (recommended for most users)

```bash
brew install jpaulorio/tap/gwtool
gwtool fetch-images        # optional: grab the sample disk-image library
```

This pulls in a bundled Greaseweazle and installs zsh/bash **completion
automatically** — no shell config needed. Images are saved under
`~/.local/share/greaseweazle-utils/disk-images` (override with `GWTOOL_IMAGES`).

> Not published yet? The tap is set up from [`PACKAGING.md`](PACKAGING.md);
> until then, use Option B.

### Option B — Git clone (development / latest)

Needs **Python 3.11+**. Greaseweazle isn't on PyPI, so it's installed from
source into a local virtualenv:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jpaulorio/greaseweazle-utils
cd greaseweazle-utils
python3.13 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install git+https://github.com/keirf/greaseweazle.git

# put gwtool on your PATH (optional; otherwise run ./bin/gwtool):
export PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH"
# enable tab-completion (optional):
echo "source $PWD/completions/gwtool.zsh" >> ~/.zshrc
```

In this mode the `.venv/` and the `disk-images/` library live inside the clone.

## 30-second start

Grammar is **machine-first**: `gwtool <machine> <action> [file]`.

```bash
gwtool info                        # is the Greaseweazle detected?
gwtool machines                    # what machines are supported?
gwtool version                     # gwtool + bundled Greaseweazle versions
gwtool about                       # credits
gwtool amiga500 backup             # read a disk -> disk-images/amiga500/
gwtool c64 restore disk-images/c64/spirit-cold-fusion.d64  # write image to disk
gwtool amiga500 flux rare-disk.scp # format-agnostic preservation capture
```

- **Backups default into `disk-images/<machine>/`** (timestamped). Pass a path
  to save elsewhere: `gwtool amiga500 backup ~/mine.adf`.
- Add `-n` to any command to preview the exact `gw` command without running it.
- **Tab-completion** (zsh/bash) completes machine → action → file. See
  [MANUAL.md](MANUAL.md#tab-completion). (`gwtool am⇥` → `amiga500`,
  then `r⇥` → `restore`.)

See **[MANUAL.md](MANUAL.md)** for everything: hardware setup, every command,
per-machine format notes and caveats, and troubleshooting.

The disk images under `disk-images/` were sourced from the Internet Archive.

# CPCPhoenix

CPCPhoenix is an Amstrad CPC 464/664/6128 emulator for Windows, written in C++.

## Features

- Z80 CPU core
- CPC system emulation: Gate Array, CRTC, PPI, PSG (AY-3-8912), FDC
- Disk (`.dsk`) and tape (`.cdt`) support
- Integrated debugger and sound analyzer
- Snapshot save/load (`.sna`)
- Copy text on the host (e.g. a BASIC listing) and paste it into the emulated CPC

## Limitations

- The emulator supports custom ROMs and RAM expansions, but there's no UI for
  adding them yet — they can only be configured in code.
- Disk and tape emulation only supports read operations. Write operations are not
  supported for now.

## Building

Open `Src\CPCPhoenix.sln` in Visual Studio 2022, pick your platform and
configuration, and build.

Output executables are named `CPCPhoenix_{Platform}_{Configuration}.exe`
(e.g. `CPCPhoenix_x64_Release.exe`).

### Runtime requirements

The system ROM files (`OS`, `BASIC` and `AMSDOS`) must be present under
`Bin\CPCPhoenix\Roms\`, relative to the executable's working directory.

Make sure your working directory is set to `Bin\CPCPhoenix\` when you run it —
otherwise CPCPhoenix won't find the ROMs.

## Command-line options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--diskA <path>` | Insert a disk image into drive A |
| `--diskA_archive <path>` | Load a disk image for drive A from an archive |
| `--diskB <path>` | Insert a disk image into drive B |
| `--diskB_archive <path>` | Load a disk image for drive B from an archive |
| `--tape <path>` | Load a tape image |
| `--autotype <text>` | Inject text into the emulated CPC |

## Thanks

Special thanks to everyone who has contributed in any form, including:

- [Daniel Varela](https://github.com/danielvarelagil2) — fixed bugs and
  improved the audio emulation

## Legal

The CPC system ROMs are redistributed with permission from Amstrad. See
[LEGAL.md](LEGAL.md) for details.
